screens.title: Virtual Private Gateway and Site-to‑Site VPN Setup
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will make sense of the Virtual Private Gateway and how AWS connects a VPC to an on‑premises network. You will learn why a VGW exists, the required steps to create and attach it, how to create a Site‑to‑Site VPN connection that links a VGW with a Customer Gateway, and how routing choices shape failover behavior. We will also cover the two IPsec tunnels AWS provisions for redundancy and how to download and interpret the AWS configuration file that you apply to your on‑premises device. By the end you will be able to explain the relationship between a VGW and a VPC, decide between static and BGP routing for a given environment, and locate the key fields in an AWS‑generated VPN configuration. For example, if your data center uses 10.0.0.0/16 you will see how to advertise or add that CIDR into the VPN configuration depending on static or dynamic routing. As you follow, notice common pitfalls like leaving a VGW detached or mismatching tunnel parameters. Ready to explore the concrete steps and configuration details that make a dependable hybrid VPN?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Virtual Private Gateway
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)

Why the VGW matters: it is the AWS‑managed VPN concentrator that becomes the logical endpoint for Site‑to‑Site VPNs to a VPC.

In this lesson
VGW
Regional, attaches to one VPC
Acts as the VPN endpoint for all Site‑to‑Site connections to that VPC.
VPN Connection
IPsec tunnels to your Customer Gateway
AWS provisions two tunnels for redundancy; each has distinct PSKs and public IPs.
Explore Key Topics
Coming up: create & attach, routing choices, download config
Create & Attach
Create VGW and attach to VPC
You must attach a VGW before it can serve VPN connections; a VPC accepts only one VGW.
Routing
Static vs Dynamic (BGP)
Static requires manual CIDR entries; BGP advertises routes automatically and aids failover.
Config File
Download and interpret
It lists AWS endpoints, PSKs, inside IPs, and example snippets for common vendors.
Visual concept
No diagram required
VGW • VPC link
A VGW is created, starts detached, then you attach it to a single VPC to make it active for VPNs.
Redundant tunnels
AWS creates two IPsec tunnels with separate public IPs and PSKs to increase availability.
Common mistake
Forgetting to attach the VGW or mismatching tunnel parameters prevents successful VPN establishment.
Key Takeaway

A VGW must be attached to a VPC before use; choose dynamic BGP for automatic route propagation and rely on the AWS config file to match tunnel parameters for your on‑premises device.

screens.title: What is a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Virtual Private Gateway is the AWS side endpoint for Site‑to‑Site VPNs and functions as the VPN concentrator for a single VPC. That means the VGW aggregates incoming VPN connections and routes traffic into the VPC's route domain. It is a regional resource and can only be attached to one VPC at a time; conversely, a VPC can have at most one VGW attached. This single‑attachment model simplifies routing and avoids ambiguity about which gateway handles VPN traffic for a VPC. A VGW begins life in a detached state after creation. The attach action links it to your VPC and allows you to create VPN connections that target it. When deciding whether to create a VGW, consider that it is the managed option for Site‑to‑Site VPNs; you will still need a Customer Gateway resource representing your on‑premises device. A common misconception is that a VGW provides internet access — it does not; it is specifically for VPN endpoints. The core takeaway: create and attach the VGW before you attempt to configure Site‑to‑Site VPNs, and remember the regional and single‑attachment constraints when designing multi‑VPC networks. How would you design a topology when multiple VPCs need VPN access?

keyIdea.text: VGW = AWS-managed VPN concentrator for a single VPC; create and attach it to enable Site‑to‑Site VPNs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What is a VGW?
Definition

Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)

A VGW is the logical AWS endpoint for Site‑to‑Site IPsec VPNs. It aggregates tunnels and routes traffic into a VPC's routing domain once attached.

Regional & attached
VGWs are regional resources and must be attached to exactly one VPC to accept VPNs.
Not an internet gateway
It is specifically for VPN endpoints; internet access requires an Internet Gateway or NAT setup.
Lifecycle
Created → detached; then attach to VPC to become active for VPN connections.
Design impact
Plan for one VGW per VPC when designing hybrid connectivity to avoid routing ambiguity.
Key Takeaway

A VGW centralizes Site‑to‑Site VPN traffic for a VPC and must be attached before you create VPN connections that target it.

Concrete example
Planning for a single VPC

If VPC A needs a Site‑to‑Site VPN, create a VGW, attach it to VPC A, then create the VPN connection using that VGW as the target gateway. Do not expect that VGW to serve VPC B unless you redesign with transit or peering patterns outside this chapter.

Misconception
A VGW is not a replacement for internet routing. It is dedicated to VPN endpoints and routing into the VPC.
Check your understanding
Why must a VGW be attached before creating a VPN connection that targets it? Consider route domain activation and the attach lifecycle.

screens.title: Create and Attach a VGW
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and attaching a VGW is a short sequence but requires attention to the ASN and attachment target. In the console you go to the VPC dashboard, choose Virtual Private Gateways, and click Create Virtual Private Gateway. The only decision at creation is the Amazon‑side ASN: you may accept the default Amazon private ASN in most cases, or provide a custom private ASN if your on‑premises BGP configuration requires it to avoid ASN conflicts. After creation the VGW will be detached. The next step is Attach to VPC — select the target VPC and confirm. Programmatically, the commands mirror the console work. For example: create the VGW with aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1 --amazon-asn 64512, capture the generated VpnGatewayId, then attach using aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway --vpn-gateway-id vgw-... --vpc-id vpc-.... After attachment, verify the VGW attachment state is attached in the console or via describe calls. A common mistake is assuming creation is enough; until you attach the VGW it cannot serve as a target for VPN connections. Try this in a lab with the default ASN first and use the attach/describe calls to validate the state.

keyIdea.title: Attach before using
keyIdea.text: Create VGW, choose ASN if needed, then attach to the target VPC; verify the attached state before creating VPN connections.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Create & Attach VGW
Process Flow

Steps to create and attach a VGW

  1. Create the VGW: choose default Amazon ASN or custom private ASN if you have BGP needs.
  2. After creation, confirm VGW state is detached; record the VpnGatewayId for CLI flows.
  3. Attach VGW to the target VPC and confirm the attachment moves to attached.
  4. Verify route tables or propagation settings later when you create the VPN connection.
ASN guidance
Default Amazon ASNs (64512 range) are fine for most setups; supply a private ASN only to match BGP planning for your network.
CLI Example
# Create a Virtual Private Gateway
aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1 --amazon-asn 64512

# Attach the VGW to your VPC
aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890 --vpc-id vpc-0123456789abcdef0
Common mistake
Assuming creation implies attachment — a detached VGW cannot be targeted by a VPN connection.
Pro tip
Record the VpnGatewayId immediately; it is used in CLI commands and logging during troubleshooting.

screens.title: Customer Gateway and Its Role
screens.narratorSegment: The Customer Gateway resource in AWS represents your on‑premises VPN device or router and provides the information AWS needs when building a Site‑to‑Site VPN connection. This resource stores the device public IP and, for dynamic routing, a BGP ASN. Creating a Customer Gateway does not configure your physical device — it merely records the parameters AWS needs to coordinate tunnel setup and BGP peering. A practical example: if your on‑premises device has public IP 203.0.113.10 and uses BGP ASN 65001, you create a Customer Gateway with those values. This enables AWS to provision tunnels targeted at that public IP and, if you choose dynamic routing, to establish BGP sessions. A common mistake is to confuse the Customer Gateway resource with actual device configuration; you must still apply the tunnel, PSKs, and IPsec settings on your device using the AWS configuration file. The Customer Gateway is essential for both static and dynamic VPNs: for static routing it provides the peer IPs and for BGP it participates in ASN exchange. After creating the CGW, you reference it when creating the VPN connection so AWS knows which on‑premises endpoint it will connect to.

keyIdea.title: Customer Gateway
keyIdea.text: CGW is an AWS representation of your on‑premises VPN device; it stores public IP and BGP ASN used when creating the VPN connection.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Customer Gateway
Definition

Customer Gateway (CGW)

A record in AWS that represents your on‑premises VPN device: it holds the device's public IP and, if using BGP, the ASN for peering.

What it stores
Public IP and BGP ASN used by AWS to provision tunnels and BGP sessions.
What it does not do
It does not configure your physical device — you must apply the settings to the device using the AWS config file.
CLI example
# Create a Customer Gateway (example)
aws ec2 create-customer-gateway --type ipsec.1 --public-ip 203.0.113.10 --bgp-asn 65001 --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=customer-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyOnPremCGW}]'

# Note: record the CustomerGatewayId for use when creating the VPN
Misconception
Creating the CGW does not push configuration to your device. It simply registers the peer details in AWS for tunnel provisioning.

screens.title: Create the Site‑to‑Site VPN Connection
screens.narratorSegment: Creating the AWS Site‑to‑Site VPN Connection links the VGW and the Customer Gateway and defines whether routing will be static or dynamic. In the console navigate to Site‑to‑Site VPN Connections and choose Create VPN Connection. Provide a descriptive name tag, select the Target Gateway by choosing the VGW you attached to your VPC, and pick the Customer Gateway resource representing your on‑premises device. The critical decision is the routing option. Select Static if your on‑premises device does not support BGP or if you prefer manual control; you must then add the on‑premises CIDRs that AWS should route to the VPN. For example, add 10.0.0.0/16 if that is your data center range. Choose Dynamic (BGP) for production networks to enable automatic route propagation and better failover. If you choose dynamic, ensure the Customer Gateway was created with a valid BGP ASN. Optionally configure tunnel options like IKE version and ciphers to match your device. Once submitted, AWS will provision the VPN and two redundant tunnels. Use CLI for automation: the create-vpn-connection call mirrors the console inputs and can be used with --options to select static routes only when needed.

keyIdea.title: VPN creation
keyIdea.text: When creating a VPN connection, select the VGW and CGW, choose routing static vs dynamic, and optionally customize tunnel options for device compatibility.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Create VPN Connection
Process

Create Site‑to‑Site VPN Connection

Define the name, target VGW, Customer Gateway, routing type, and optional tunnel options to match your on‑premises device.

Name Tag
Use a descriptive name like MyHybridConn-VPC1 to keep resources clear in the console.
Target & Customer Gateway
Select the attached VGW and the CGW resource representing the on‑premises peer.
CLI Example
# Create the VPN Connection with dynamic BGP
aws ec2 create-vpn-connection \
    --type ipsec.1 \
    --customer-gateway-id cgw-0fedcba9876543210 \
    --vpn-gateway-id vgw-0abcdef1234567890 \
    --options '{"StaticRoutesOnly":false}' \
    --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpn-connection,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=MyHybridVPN}]'

# For static routing, set StaticRoutesOnly to true and add routes
Routing decision
Choose dynamic BGP for automatic route propagation and failover; static when your device lacks BGP support or you require manual control.

screens.title: Routing Options: Static vs Dynamic (BGP)
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing static or dynamic routing is one of the most important design decisions when creating a Site‑to‑Site VPN. Static routing requires you to manually list the on‑premises CIDR blocks in the VPN configuration so AWS knows which destinations are reachable via the tunnel. Static is simple and suitable when your on‑premises device does not support BGP or when you have a small, stable set of prefixes. The drawback is failover: if one tunnel fails you must manually reroute or rely on device‑level policies to shift traffic. Dynamic routing uses BGP to automatically exchange routes between AWS and your Customer Gateway. Its primary benefit is automatic route propagation and failover: when a tunnel goes down BGP withdraws routes, letting the healthy tunnel carry traffic without manual intervention. For production networks the recommendation is dynamic BGP for resilience. A misconception is that BGP makes encryption stronger — it does not; both options use IPsec for encryption. Instead, BGP improves operational reliability and reduces manual configuration. When planning, ensure your CGW has a valid ASN if you pick dynamic routing. Routing Options: Static vs Dynamic (BGP) means static routing is manual but simple; dynamic bgp automates route exchange and failover and is recommended for production.. In practical terms, tradeoffs, when to choose each, and practical implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Routing tradeoff
keyIdea.text: Static routing is manual but simple; dynamic BGP automates route exchange and failover and is recommended for production.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Static vs Dynamic
Static Routing

Manual CIDR configuration

  • You manually add on‑premises CIDR blocks (for example 10.0.0.0/16) to the VPN connection.
  • Useful for devices without BGP or small stable networks.
  • Failover is manual unless your device handles path selection automatically.
Dynamic Routing (BGP)

Automatic route exchange

  • BGP advertises routes between the Customer Gateway and the VGW.
  • Automatic failover: BGP withdraws routes when a tunnel fails so traffic moves to the healthy tunnel.
  • Requires the Customer Gateway to have a valid BGP ASN recorded.
Comparison example
If your data center uses 10.0.0.0/16 and you choose static routing, add that CIDR to the VPN configuration so AWS routes it to the tunnel. If you choose BGP, the on‑premises router advertises 10.0.0.0/16 and AWS learns it automatically.

screens.title: Tunnel Options and IPsec Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Tunnel options control the IPsec parameters used for each VPN tunnel. AWS provisions two tunnels by default and offers default secure values, but you may need to customize IKE version, pre‑shared keys, Diffie‑Hellman groups, encryption algorithms like AES‑128 or AES‑256, and hash algorithms such as SHA1 or SHA256. It is common to let AWS generate pre‑shared keys, but some environments require you to provide them so both ends match. Older on‑premises hardware may only support IKEv1 or weaker ciphers, so tailoring tunnel options is sometimes required. Another important setting is tunnel lifetime — both IKE and IPsec have lifetimes that determine when keys rekey; these should be compatible at both ends. A practical troubleshooting tip is to compare the AWS configuration file values for Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters with your device configuration; mismatches in DH group or encryption/hash are a frequent cause of tunnel failure. Use the strongest mutually supported algorithms, and when you change tunnel options test in a non‑production environment first. Remember each tunnel also has a unique pre‑shared key and public IP address on the AWS side.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Tunnel Options
Tunnel Options

IPsec Parameters to match

IKE version
IKEv1 or IKEv2 — choose based on device support.
Pre‑shared key
AWS generates unique PSKs per tunnel or you can specify your own; keep them secure.
Diffie‑Hellman group
Select compatible DH groups for key exchange strength.
Encryption & Hash
AES‑128/256 and SHA1/SHA256 are common choices; prefer the strongest mutually supported algorithms.
Why this matters
A mismatch in any of these parameters between AWS and your device will prevent the IPsec tunnels from establishing, creating a prolonged outage if not caught early.
Check before applying
  • Compare Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters from the AWS config file with your device.
  • Use the strongest algorithms both ends support.
  • Test changes in a non‑production environment first.
Common mistake
Failing to update the device to match AWS defaults or custom tunnel options is a frequent root cause of failed tunnels.

screens.title: Redundant IPsec Tunnels and Failover
screens.narratorSegment: AWS provisions two independent IPsec tunnels for each VPN connection. Each tunnel has its own public IP on the VGW side and its own pre‑shared key. This design enables high availability: if one tunnel experiences an internet outage or endpoint problem, the other tunnel remains a viable path. With dynamic routing using BGP this failover is automatic — BGP notices the failed path, withdraws the affected routes, and the remaining tunnel carries the advertised prefixes. With static routing the redundancy still exists but failover requires manual reconfiguration or device‑level path selection because AWS will not automatically withdraw static routes; you must plan how your device prefers one tunnel over the other or implement local policies. Another important detail is that AWS may provision unique inside tunnel IP addresses for each tunnel. When troubleshooting, gather the two AWS public IPs and PSKs from the configuration file and test each tunnel independently. A common misconception is that two tunnels mean simultaneous load balancing by default; unless BGP or device policies are configured to load share, the tunnels provide standby redundancy rather than automatic traffic splitting.

keyIdea.text: Two independent tunnels provide high availability; BGP automates failover, while static routing may require manual intervention.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Redundant Tunnels
Availability

Two IPsec tunnels per connection

Each VPN connection includes two independently provisioned tunnels. Each tunnel has a unique AWS public IP and a unique pre‑shared key. This redundancy improves resilience by providing an alternate path if one tunnel fails.

With BGP, failover is automatic because BGP withdraws routes for the failed tunnel. With static routing, manual intervention or device policies are required to move traffic to the healthy tunnel.

Do not assume automatic load balancing across the two tunnels unless you explicitly configure BGP or device side policies that support multipath behavior.

Troubleshooting checklist
  • Collect both AWS VGW public IPs and PSKs from the config file.
  • Test tunnel establishment one at a time to isolate issues.
  • If BGP is used, verify BGP sessions and route advertisements.
Misconception
Two tunnels provide high availability but not automatic traffic splitting unless you configure routing to do so.

screens.title: Download and Interpret the AWS Configuration File
screens.narratorSegment: After you create the VPN connection AWS enters a pending state and generates a configuration file specific to many popular vendor platforms. This file contains the two AWS VGW public IP addresses—one per tunnel—the two unique pre‑shared keys, the inside tunnel IP addresses for both the VGW and the Customer Gateway, and detailed Phase 1 and Phase 2 IPsec parameters. It also often includes example configuration snippets for BGP or static routes. Programmatically you can identify supported device types with get-vpn-connection-device-types and retrieve a sample configuration with get-vpn-connection-device-sample-configuration. Once you download the file, extract the public IPs and PSKs and apply the matching IKE and IPsec parameters to your on‑premises appliance. A common error is to skip reviewing the inside tunnel IPs used for BGP next‑hop or static route configuration; those inside addresses are required when setting up BGP peering or adding static route next-hops. Securely store the pre‑shared keys and test the tunnels in a lab environment to validate the parameters before applying them in production. Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Download Configuration
What to download

AWS-generated VPN configuration

The file provides vendor-specific snippets and the exact parameters required to configure your on‑premises VPN device for each of the two tunnels.

Key fields
AWS public IPs, PSKs, inside tunnel IPs, Phase 1/2 parameters, and sample BGP/static configuration.
Where to download
Select the VPN connection in the console and choose Download Configuration; select Generic if your vendor is not listed.
CLI example
# Identify supported device types
aws ec2 get-vpn-connection-device-types --vpn-connection-id vpn-0123456789abcdef0

# Download a sample configuration for the selected device type
aws ec2 get-vpn-connection-device-sample-configuration \
    --vpn-connection-id vpn-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --vpn-connection-device-type-id vpn-connection-device-type-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --output text > MyOnPremVPNConfig.txt
Practical tip
Open the file and copy the AWS public IPs, inside IPs, and PSKs into your device configuration; then validate each tunnel separately before enabling BGP or traffic flows.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of recurring mistakes when setting up VGWs and VPN connections. First, forgetting to attach the VGW is common; a detached VGW cannot be used as a VPN target, so always attach and confirm the attached state. Second, choosing the wrong routing option — for instance selecting static when you need BGP — leads to stale routes or manual failover work. If you choose static routing, remember to add your on‑premises CIDRs; if you choose dynamic, ensure your Customer Gateway has a valid BGP ASN. Third, mismatched tunnel options between AWS and your device prevent tunnels from establishing. Always compare Phase 1 and Phase 2 settings, PSKs, and inside tunnel IPs against the AWS configuration file. Fourth, not downloading or relying on the AWS generated configuration and instead configuring by memory introduces subtle errors. Safety notes: keep pre‑shared keys secure, test changes in a non‑production environment when possible, and be cautious when modifying route tables since propagation and route changes can affect live traffic. These practices reduce outage risk and speed troubleshooting when problems occur. Common setup mistakes

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will make sense of the Virtual Private Gateway and how AWS connects a VPC to an on‑premises network. You will learn why a VGW exists, the required steps to create and attach it, how to create a Site‑to‑Site VPN connection that links a VGW with a Customer Gateway, and how routing choices shape failover behavior. We will also cover the two IPsec tunnels AWS provisions for redundancy and how to download and interpret the AWS configuration file that you apply to your on‑premises device. By the end you will be able to explain the relationship between a VGW and a VPC, decide between static and BGP routing for a given environment, and locate the key fields in an AWS‑generated VPN configuration. For example, if your data center uses 10.0.0.0/16 you will see how to advertise or add that CIDR into the VPN configuration depending on static or dynamic routing. As you follow, notice common pitfalls like leaving a VGW detached or mismatching tunnel parameters. Ready to explore the concrete steps and configuration details that make a dependable hybrid VPN?

These learning objectives describe practical skills you'll gain when working with Virtual Private Gateways and Site‑to‑Site VPNs. First, you will explain the function of a VGW and its relationship with a VPC, including the fact that a VGW is regional and attaches to only one VPC at a time — this is important for planning network topology. Second, you will walk through the exact steps to create a VGW, choose an ASN when necessary, and attach it to an existing VPC so it can be used as a VPN endpoint. Third, you will configure an AWS Site‑to‑Site VPN connection by selecting the Customer Gateway, naming the connection, and deciding between static or dynamic routing. Finally, you will learn to verify that the VGW reports as attached and that the VPN connection moves to an active state after both tunnels establish. Each objective is tied to a concrete action you can perform in the console or via the CLI, which helps you move from concept to validated setup in a lab or production environment.

This second objectives screen breaks the chapter into actionable skills you can test in a lab. First, you will choose an ASN for a VGW when needed and know when the default Amazon ASN is acceptable — understanding this prevents BGP ASN conflicts. Second, you will know how to verify VGW attachment status and the implications of the one‑VGW‑per‑VPC constraint when planning multiple VPCs. Third, you will be able to select and document tunnel options to match your on‑premises device, including IKE version, pre‑shared keys, Diffie‑Hellman groups, and algorithms; matching parameters is a frequent troubleshooting step. Fourth, you will practice downloading and reading the AWS configuration file to extract the AWS VGW public IPs, PSKs, inside tunnel IPs, and sample BGP or static config snippets. These skills are practical: they prevent misconfiguration, speed up troubleshooting, and ensure your VPN comes up consistently when you test in a non‑production environment before rolling to production.

A Virtual Private Gateway is the AWS side endpoint for Site‑to‑Site VPNs and functions as the VPN concentrator for a single VPC. That means the VGW aggregates incoming VPN connections and routes traffic into the VPC's route domain. It is a regional resource and can only be attached to one VPC at a time; conversely, a VPC can have at most one VGW attached. This single‑attachment model simplifies routing and avoids ambiguity about which gateway handles VPN traffic for a VPC. A VGW begins life in a detached state after creation. The attach action links it to your VPC and allows you to create VPN connections that target it. When deciding whether to create a VGW, consider that it is the managed option for Site‑to‑Site VPNs; you will still need a Customer Gateway resource representing your on‑premises device. A common misconception is that a VGW provides internet access — it does not; it is specifically for VPN endpoints. The core takeaway: create and attach the VGW before you attempt to configure Site‑to‑Site VPNs, and remember the regional and single‑attachment constraints when designing multi‑VPC networks. How would you design a topology when multiple VPCs need VPN access?

Creating and attaching a VGW is a short sequence but requires attention to the ASN and attachment target. In the console you go to the VPC dashboard, choose Virtual Private Gateways, and click Create Virtual Private Gateway. The only decision at creation is the Amazon‑side ASN: you may accept the default Amazon private ASN in most cases, or provide a custom private ASN if your on‑premises BGP configuration requires it to avoid ASN conflicts. After creation the VGW will be detached. The next step is Attach to VPC — select the target VPC and confirm. Programmatically, the commands mirror the console work. For example: create the VGW with aws ec2 create-vpn-gateway --type ipsec.1 --amazon-asn 64512, capture the generated VpnGatewayId, then attach using aws ec2 attach-vpn-gateway --vpn-gateway-id vgw-... --vpc-id vpc-.... After attachment, verify the VGW attachment state is attached in the console or via describe calls. A common mistake is assuming creation is enough; until you attach the VGW it cannot serve as a target for VPN connections. Try this in a lab with the default ASN first and use the attach/describe calls to validate the state.

The Customer Gateway resource in AWS represents your on‑premises VPN device or router and provides the information AWS needs when building a Site‑to‑Site VPN connection. This resource stores the device public IP and, for dynamic routing, a BGP ASN. Creating a Customer Gateway does not configure your physical device — it merely records the parameters AWS needs to coordinate tunnel setup and BGP peering. A practical example: if your on‑premises device has public IP 203.0.113.10 and uses BGP ASN 65001, you create a Customer Gateway with those values. This enables AWS to provision tunnels targeted at that public IP and, if you choose dynamic routing, to establish BGP sessions. A common mistake is to confuse the Customer Gateway resource with actual device configuration; you must still apply the tunnel, PSKs, and IPsec settings on your device using the AWS configuration file. The Customer Gateway is essential for both static and dynamic VPNs: for static routing it provides the peer IPs and for BGP it participates in ASN exchange. After creating the CGW, you reference it when creating the VPN connection so AWS knows which on‑premises endpoint it will connect to.

Creating the AWS Site‑to‑Site VPN Connection links the VGW and the Customer Gateway and defines whether routing will be static or dynamic. In the console navigate to Site‑to‑Site VPN Connections and choose Create VPN Connection. Provide a descriptive name tag, select the Target Gateway by choosing the VGW you attached to your VPC, and pick the Customer Gateway resource representing your on‑premises device. The critical decision is the routing option. Select Static if your on‑premises device does not support BGP or if you prefer manual control; you must then add the on‑premises CIDRs that AWS should route to the VPN. For example, add 10.0.0.0/16 if that is your data center range. Choose Dynamic (BGP) for production networks to enable automatic route propagation and better failover. If you choose dynamic, ensure the Customer Gateway was created with a valid BGP ASN. Optionally configure tunnel options like IKE version and ciphers to match your device. Once submitted, AWS will provision the VPN and two redundant tunnels. Use CLI for automation: the create-vpn-connection call mirrors the console inputs and can be used with --options to select static routes only when needed.

Choosing static or dynamic routing is one of the most important design decisions when creating a Site‑to‑Site VPN. Static routing requires you to manually list the on‑premises CIDR blocks in the VPN configuration so AWS knows which destinations are reachable via the tunnel. Static is simple and suitable when your on‑premises device does not support BGP or when you have a small, stable set of prefixes. The drawback is failover: if one tunnel fails you must manually reroute or rely on device‑level policies to shift traffic. Dynamic routing uses BGP to automatically exchange routes between AWS and your Customer Gateway. Its primary benefit is automatic route propagation and failover: when a tunnel goes down BGP withdraws routes, letting the healthy tunnel carry traffic without manual intervention. For production networks the recommendation is dynamic BGP for resilience. A misconception is that BGP makes encryption stronger — it does not; both options use IPsec for encryption. Instead, BGP improves operational reliability and reduces manual configuration. When planning, ensure your CGW has a valid ASN if you pick dynamic routing. Routing Options: Static vs Dynamic (BGP) means static routing is manual but simple; dynamic bgp automates route exchange and failover and is recommended for production.. In practical terms, tradeoffs, when to choose each, and practical implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tunnel options control the IPsec parameters used for each VPN tunnel. AWS provisions two tunnels by default and offers default secure values, but you may need to customize IKE version, pre‑shared keys, Diffie‑Hellman groups, encryption algorithms like AES‑128 or AES‑256, and hash algorithms such as SHA1 or SHA256. It is common to let AWS generate pre‑shared keys, but some environments require you to provide them so both ends match. Older on‑premises hardware may only support IKEv1 or weaker ciphers, so tailoring tunnel options is sometimes required. Another important setting is tunnel lifetime — both IKE and IPsec have lifetimes that determine when keys rekey; these should be compatible at both ends. A practical troubleshooting tip is to compare the AWS configuration file values for Phase 1 and Phase 2 parameters with your device configuration; mismatches in DH group or encryption/hash are a frequent cause of tunnel failure. Use the strongest mutually supported algorithms, and when you change tunnel options test in a non‑production environment first. Remember each tunnel also has a unique pre‑shared key and public IP address on the AWS side.

AWS provisions two independent IPsec tunnels for each VPN connection. Each tunnel has its own public IP on the VGW side and its own pre‑shared key. This design enables high availability: if one tunnel experiences an internet outage or endpoint problem, the other tunnel remains a viable path. With dynamic routing using BGP this failover is automatic — BGP notices the failed path, withdraws the affected routes, and the remaining tunnel carries the advertised prefixes. With static routing the redundancy still exists but failover requires manual reconfiguration or device‑level path selection because AWS will not automatically withdraw static routes; you must plan how your device prefers one tunnel over the other or implement local policies. Another important detail is that AWS may provision unique inside tunnel IP addresses for each tunnel. When troubleshooting, gather the two AWS public IPs and PSKs from the configuration file and test each tunnel independently. A common misconception is that two tunnels mean simultaneous load balancing by default; unless BGP or device policies are configured to load share, the tunnels provide standby redundancy rather than automatic traffic splitting.

After you create the VPN connection AWS enters a pending state and generates a configuration file specific to many popular vendor platforms. There are a handful of recurring mistakes when setting up VGWs and VPN connections. First, forgetting to attach the VGW is common; a detached VGW cannot be used as a VPN target, so always attach and confirm the attached state. Second, choosing the wrong routing option — for instance selecting static when you need BGP — leads to stale routes or manual failover work. If you choose static routing, remember to add your on‑premises CIDRs; if you choose dynamic, ensure your Customer Gateway has a valid BGP ASN. Third, mismatched tunnel options between AWS and your device prevent tunnels from establishing. Always compare Phase 1 and Phase 2 settings, PSKs, and inside tunnel IPs against the AWS configuration file. Fourth, not downloading or relying on the AWS generated configuration and instead configuring by memory introduces subtle errors. Safety notes: keep pre‑shared keys secure, test changes in a non‑production environment when possible, and be cautious when modifying route tables since propagation and route changes can affect live traffic. These practices reduce outage risk and speed troubleshooting when problems occur.
